title: Ang 151: Gauri begins
hook: the Granth's largest raga opens with Guru Nanak
tomorrow: how do you lose a whole day without noticing?

segments.voice: A week in Majh. Family, on ang 103. The long run of hymns on the stubborn I. Closing hymns, with a hidden jewel. Your month. The majh ballad and its bright line. And yesterday, the ballad ends, with a mosque of mercy. Now a new raga.
screen: `FAMILY · THE LONG RUN · CLOSING HYMNS.` → `YOUR MONTH · THE MAJH BALLAD · THE BALLAD ENDS.` → `A NEW RAGA.`

segments.voice: A moving box full of books. A sleeping kid carried up the stairs. A grandparent's hand, when they lean on you for the first time. Heavy things come in different shapes. So what's heavier than anything you've ever lifted? Gauri opens on ang 151, and Guru Nanak's first line in it weighs two things against each other.
screen: `A BOX OF BOOKS. A SLEEPING KID.` → `HEAVY COMES IN SHAPES.` → `GAURI WEIGHS TWO THINGS.`

segments.voice: Gauri runs from ang 151 all the way to 346, the largest raga in the Granth, and Guru Nanak opens it with a scale. In paraphrase: the fear of God is very heavy, a great weight; the mind's own cleverness is light, and it speaks light words. Bhau, the word here, is fear, but not the kind that makes you run. It's closer to awe: the weight of standing before something real, the kind that makes you careful. And the clever mind? It's quick and it's light, and it talks. That's the contrast. Light talk floats. Awe sits down in you and stays. Notice how this week fits the scale. A protector everywhere, so fear of anything else runs out. An I that's given away. A jewel kept hidden. A month for clean hands. Another's due, off the plate. A mosque made of mercy. None of it is clever. All of it is heavy, in the good way, the way a hand on your shoulder is heavy.
screen: `GAURI: ANG 151 TO 346.` · `AWE IS HEAVY.` · `CLEVERNESS IS LIGHT, AND TALKS.` · `A WEEK OF GOOD WEIGHT.` · then, large: `THE LARGEST RAGA.`

segments.voice: If you can, open ang 151 and read the first line aloud, slowly. Then say two words out loud, one at a time: first light, then heavy. Notice which one your body settles into, and stay there for the rest of the sit.
Ang 151. The page where Gauri begins, with Guru Nanak weighing awe against cleverness.
Last line of the week: the largest raga, opening on something heavy. A new raga, and a long one.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading the Granth in order reach Gauri after Majh ki Var; Gauri hymns are sung in kirtan, and the long Sukhmani, read daily by some Sikhs, sits inside this raga.
